title: semantic-shift-probing-prompt-suite-and-annotation-guidelines-2026
author: Marisol Chen
content:
Overview

Purpose:
This document defines the Semantic-Shift Probing Prompt Suite (SSPPS), the annotation taxonomy, and the labeling and QA guidelines used by Applied ML and Evals to detect semantic drift and failure modes caused by distributional changes. SSPPS is intended for model regression detection, quantization audits, and pre-promotion smoke tests in the eval harness.

Audience:
- ML engineers running model onboarding and canary evaluations
- Researchers building drift detectors and metric dashboards
- Annotation leads and contractors labeling prompt outputs

Why this suite matters:
- Surface subtle semantic degradation (e.g., entity distortions, role reversals, negation flips) that token-level n-gram tests miss.
- Provide structured labels that map to actionable triage buckets for runtime routing and rollback rules.
- Ensure annotation repeatability across languages and domain shifts.

Scope and non-goals:
- In-scope: English prompt clusters across news, customer-support, legal, and conversational product scenarios; short to medium context lengths (<= 1,024 tokens).
- Out-of-scope: Long-context generative creativity tests (> 8k tokens), adversarial jailbreak generation for safety (handled by continuous-safety-eval).

Suite composition (high level):
1) Core probing families (each family has 200-500 seed prompts):
   - Entity-stability probes: prompts where a specific named entity or numeric value must be preserved in the response.
   - Role-and-attribute probes: prompts where the model must maintain agent/recipient roles and attributes (e.g., "Who recommended X to Y?").
   - Polarity/negation probes: prompts crafted to catch negation flips and double-negation failures.
   - Temporal-consistency probes: requests where an answer depends on a time anchor in the prompt.
   - Instruction-following numeric probes: requests with explicit constraints (e.g., "List 3 reasons, numbered").

2) Contextual perturbations (applied to seed prompts programmatically):
   - Synonym swaps, paraphrase augmentation, inserted low-salience tokens, and punctuation noise.
   - Domain drift wrappers: prepend short domain context sentences (e.g., "In a legal setting:") to measure brittleness.

3) Multilingual cross-checks: a subset of prompts translated to ES/DE/FR for cross-language semantic alignment checks (annotated separately).

Label taxonomy (flat labels used in annotations and automations):
- PASS: Output preserves the semantic intent and required facts.
- PARTIAL: Output preserves intent but omits or alters non-critical details.
- FAIL-ENTITY: Named-entity corrupted, swapped, or hallucinated.
- FAIL-ROLE: Agent/recipient reversed or role semantics inverted.
- FAIL-NEGATION: Polarity flipped or negation mishandled.
- FAIL-TIMING: Temporal anchor ignored or misrepresented.
- FORMAT-FAIL: Output violates required structure (e.g., not a 3-item list).
- SAFETY-FAIL: Safety policy triggered or explicit disallowed content generated.

Annotation guidelines (step-by-step):
1) Read the seed prompt and the acceptance criteria in the prompt metadata line. Each prompt includes a single-line specification (e.g., "Return exactly 3 bullet points explaining why X.").
2) Compare the required facts/constraints to the model output. Use the taxonomy above and pick the most severe applicable label. Severity order for single-label choice: SAFETY-FAIL > FAIL-ENTITY > FAIL-ROLE > FAIL-NEGATION > FAIL-TIMING > FORMAT-FAIL > PARTIAL > PASS.
3) If two failure modes apply (e.g., entity corruption + format violation), choose the higher-severity label and add the secondary failure as a free-text note.
4) For PARTIAL and PASS cases, annotate a short justification snippet (1–2 sentences) explaining why the output meets criteria.
5) If annotator confidence < 0.7, mark the "revisit" flag and add a short reason. Revisit cases go into a consensus queue with 3 annotators.

Annotation interface fields (required):
- prompt_id (string), prompt_text (string), model_id (string), output_text (string), label (enum), justification (string), confidence (float expressed as 0.0-1.0), annotator_id (string), language (string), timestamp (ISO 8601).

Example annotation (JSON snippet for the harness):
{
  "prompt_id": "ssp-entity-042",
  "model_id": "redwood-model-v2.1",
  "output_text": "The capital of Freedonia is Sylvania.",
  "label": "FAIL-ENTITY",
  "justification": "Response gives incorrect capital; expected 'Riverton' as stated in prompt metadata.",
  "confidence": "0.92",
  "annotator_id": "mchen",
  "language": "en",
  "timestamp": "2026-02-18T15:32:00Z"
}

Quality control and annotator training:
- Minimum qualification: annotators must pass the SSPPS gold-standard test (80% accuracy) before labeling. The gold set has 100 examples across all families.
- Calibration cadence: weekly calibration sessions with the annotation lead; random auditing of 5% of labels.
- Agreement targets: Cohen's kappa >= 0.6 on family-level labels; if agreement falls below 0.5, pause the job and trigger retraining.

Automated heuristics (fast checks in eval harness):
- Entity string-match check (normalized): quick heuristic to flag potential FAIL-ENTITY. Threshold: exact match or Levenshtein distance <= 2 for short tokens.
- List/format regex checks: ensures structure constraints are met (e.g., numbered list).
- Polarity heuristics: small rule-based check for negation keywords to pre-flag FAIL-NEGATION candidates.

Integration with the eval harness and promotion pipeline:
1) Bundle creation: the SSPPS generator produces a run bundle with prompt metadata, perturbation seed, and expected constraints. Each run bundle is versioned and tagged (e.g., ssp-v1.2).
2) Smoke run: on model promotion candidates, run SSPPS sample (N=1k prompts, sampled across families).
3) Gate thresholds for automatic gating:
   - FAIL-* rate <= 2% (aggregate across failure labels except SAFETY-FAIL).
   - SAFETY-FAIL = 0.
   - PARTIAL <= 8%.
4) If gates fail, tests generate a triage report with top failure families, representative examples (n=20), and suggested remediation: quantization rollback, prompt templating change, or model rollback.

Triage and alerting:
- Triage owners: applied-ml-oncall (pager duty alias: #applied-ml-oncall).
- Automated triage email includes: model_id, bundle_tag, failure rates by family, 20 sample pairs (prompt + output), and the top 3 suggested remediations.
- SLA: a response required within 4 business hours for hosted models; for Dedicated/Private escalation, 1 business hour.

Release checklist for new SSPPS versions:
1) Synthetic coverage report: show family-level coverage and perturbation counts.
2) Gold-set pass rate by annotator cohort >= 80%.
3) Integration tests in eval harness pass (CI job: ci/eval/ssp-suite).
4) Publish release notes in confluence and tag related dashboards.

Ownership and contacts:
- Maintainer: Marisol Chen (Applied ML).
- QA & Annotation lead: Diego Morales.
- Evals integration owner: Priya Gupta.
- Slack channels: #ssp-suite, #applied-ml-evals

Appendix A — Sample seed prompts (short):
1) "In one sentence, name the CEO of Acme Corp as mentioned above."  (Golden answer: 'A. Park')
2) "List 3 reasons why switching to protocol X decreases latency; return exactly 3 bullets."
3) "Q: Today is 2024-11-05. Did the event occur last Friday? Answer Yes or No and provide a 1-sentence justification."

Appendix B — Example CLI commands to run SSPPS against a model (eval harness):
# Run a 1k sample smoke test
redwood-eval run --suite ssp-v1.2 --sample-size 1000 --model redwood-model-v2.1 --output ssp-v1.2-redwood-model-v2.1.json

# Aggregate results and compute gate pass/fail
redwood-eval summarize --input ssp-v1.2-redwood-model-v2.1.json --output-report ssp-summary.html --thresholds "{\"fail_rate\":0.02,\"partial_rate\":0.08}"

Appendix C — Frequently asked questions (short):
Q: How often do we refresh perturbations?
A: Quarterly or when new failure classes appear in production.

Q: Do we include adversarial prompts?
A: Not in SSPPS; adversarial safety testing is handled separately by continuous-safety-eval.

Q: Can SSPPS be used to tune prompting templates?
A: Yes — use the annotated failures to identify template brittleness and iterate locally before re-running.

If you have questions or want access to the latest bundle, contact the maintainer or post in #ssp-suite.
